learn.title: Main first
learn.body: The compiler reads from top to bottom. If `main` calls a function the compiler has not seen yet, it complains. A prototype solves this: a one-line promise that the function exists, with the same type information as the definition.

learn.title: A prototype
learn.body: The prototype is the line ending in a semicolon, above `main`.

learn.title: Why use them
learn.body: With prototypes at the top, you can put `main` first, so the reader sees the story before the details. A prototype is the definition's first line with a semicolon instead of a body. Parameter names are optional in it, but keep them for clarity.

learn.title: Scope
learn.body: A variable only exists inside the braces where it is declared. This is its scope. A variable declared in a function is local to that function and disappears when the function ends. Other functions cannot see it.

learn.title: Two different n
learn.body: Each function has its own `n`, so they do not clash.

learn.title: Reading the program
learn.body: Both functions declare a variable called `n`.
steps: `show()` creates a separate `n` holding 2, and prints 2
Back in `main`, its `n` is still 1, so it prints 1

learn.body: A variable declared outside every function is global and visible everywhere. Avoid globals. They make bugs hard to find.

choices: A one-line declaration of a function before its definition
questions.explanation: It tells the compiler the name, parameters and return type.
A prototype has no body, so it ends with `;`.

questions.prompt: The part of a program where a variable exists is called its \_\_.
questions.explanation: Scope is set by the braces around the declaration.

questions.prompt: In the two-`n` program, what does the second line print, from `main`? Type the number.
questions.explanation: `main`'s own `n` was never changed, so it is still 1.

questions.prompt: Can `main` use a variable declared inside `show`?
choices: Yes, if it is an int
questions.explanation: Local variables are invisible outside their function.

questions.prompt: Why would you add a prototype above `main`?
choices: To make the program run faster
questions.explanation: The compiler learns the function exists before main calls it.

questions.prompt: What does the prototype `int twice(int n);` say?
choices: twice takes an int and returns an int
questions.explanation: The first `int` is the return type and the one in parentheses is the parameter.

questions.prompt: Put the pieces of a program in order.
questions.explanation: Includes, then prototypes, then main, then the definitions.
